newsitem.title: USA: Ex-detective in Simpson case pleads no-contest.
newsitem.headline: Ex-detective in Simpson case pleads no-contest.

text.p: Former police detective Mark Fuhrman pleaded no-contest on Wednesday to a charge that he committed perjury at the O.J. Simpson murder trial when he testified he had not used a racial slur anytime in the past decade.

Only hours after first declaring his innocence, Fuhrman -- a key investigator in the murders of Simpson's ex-wife and her friend -- changed his plea in a deal with prosecutors under which he avoided jail time and received three years' probation and a $200 fine.
If convicted on the felony perjury charge, Fuhrman could have been sentenced to several years behind bars.
Before approving the plea bargain, Superior Court Judge Judge John Ouderkirk told Fuhrman the no-contest plea amounted to an admission of guilt under California law.
The criminal case against Fuhrman, who retired in late 1995 and now lives in Idaho, stemmed from an 11-month investigation by the California attorney general's office.

The perjury charge was filed one year to the day after a mostly black jury acquitted Simpson, a former football star and actor, in the killings of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman. The jury deliberated for less than three hours.

Fuhrman was accused of lying on the witness stand on March 15, 1995, when he testified that "he had not addressed any black person as a 'nigger' or spoken about black people as 'niggers' in the past 10 years," according to a criminal complaint.
Following his testimony, an aspiring screenwriter came forward with taped interviews with Fuhrman in which he uttered the racial slur dozens of times.

When Fuhrman was called back to the witness stand, he invoked his constitutional right against self-incrimination and refused to answer questions. The defence built its case around claims that Fuhrman was a racist who planted a bloody glove found at the black celebrity's estate after the murders.
Fuhrman said little during the hearing and spoke almost in a whisper when answering the judge's questions. He left the courtroom through a side door guarded by officers.
